title: Ten, ta, to — the three noun genders
title_target: Ten stół, ta lampa, to okno
goal: Recognize a noun's gender from its ending, point things out with *ten / ta / to*, and count to twenty.
bekal: guess a noun's gender from its last letter, right more than nine times out of ten
ask *co to jest?* and answer it

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Co to jest?
dialogs.intro: The classroom after the lesson. Ania points at things around the room; Budi guesses their names.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: It's a book. A Polish book.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: To jest… nie wiem. Jak to się nazywa po polsku?
lines.id: It's a… I don't know. What's it called in Polish?
lines.literal: this is… not I-know. how this self names in-Polish?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: To jest okno. Okno jest duże.
lines.id: It's a window. The window is big.
lines.literal: this is window. window is big.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aha. A ten stół? Ten stół jest mały.
lines.id: Oh. And this table? This table is small.
lines.literal: aha. and this-m table? this-m table is small.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Tak! Ten stół, ta lampa, to okno.
lines.id: Yes! Ten stół, ta lampa, to okno.
lines.literal: yes! this-m table, this-f lamp, this-n window.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dlaczego ten, ta i to? Nie rozumiem.
lines.id: Why ten, ta, and to? I don't understand.
lines.literal: why ten, ta and to? not I-understand.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Bo każdy rzeczownik ma rodzaj: męski, żeński albo nijaki.
lines.id: Because every noun has a gender: masculine, feminine, or neuter.
lines.literal: because every noun has gender: masculine, feminine or neuter.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And how do you tell the gender?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Popatrz na koniec słowa. To cała tajemnica.
lines.id: Look at the end of the word. That's the whole secret.
lines.literal: look at end of-word. this whole secret.

notes: **To jest… works for anything.** When introducing a thing — of any gender — the sentence is always *to jest*, never *ten jest* or *ta jest*. *To jest książka*, *to jest stół*, *to jest okno*. This is the biggest shortcut in the unit: as long as you're just **pointing**, you don't need to know the gender at all.
**What changes is *ten / ta / to* when it's attached to the noun.** Compare: *To jest stół* (this is a table) and *Ten stół jest mały* (this table is small). The first points; the second describes.

**Jest can disappear.** *To cała tajemnica* in the last line has no *jest*, and it's still a complete sentence. In short sentences that equate two things, *jest* is often simply dropped — something English never allows.

**Nie wiem** (I don't know) is one of the sentences you'll use most in your first months. Its partner: *nie rozumiem* (I don't understand). *Wiedzieć* is knowing a **fact**; for knowing a **person**, Polish uses *znać*.
**Jak to się nazywa po polsku?** Lifesaver phrase number one. Memorize it whole, don't take it apart — it will replace a dictionary in many situations.

**Adjectives come first.** *Polska książka* (a Polish book), *duże okno* (a big window) — same as English. Notice too that the adjective's ending follows the noun's gender: *mały stół*, *mała lampa*, *małe okno*.
**Bo** means "because" and always sits in the middle of the sentence. To start a sentence with "because", use *ponieważ*, which sounds more formal.

grammars.title: The three noun genders — and how to guess them
body: Every Polish noun has one of three genders. The good news: the gender can almost always be read from the **last letter**, so there's no need to memorize each one like German *der/die/das*.
after: This rule works for more than nine nouns out of ten. The exceptions you'll really meet come in just two groups: words ending in *-ość* (*miłość*, *radość*), which are **żeński** despite ending in a consonant, and words like *mężczyzna* (man), *kolega* (friend), *tata* (dad), which end in *-a* but are **męski** because they mean male people.
⚠️ Gender here is a matter of **grammar**, not meaning. *Stół* (table) isn't male in any sense; it just belongs to the group whose endings behave that way. Don't look for reasons; look at the ending.

Why does this matter right now? Because noun gender decides almost every other ending in Polish: adjectives, "this/that", possessives, and the noun's own shape in the six other noun forms. Guess the gender wrong here and the mistake spreads to every unit that follows.

grammars.title: Ten, ta, to — and their twins
body: The pointing word follows the noun's gender, and there are only two plural forms.
after: For "that" (far away) there's *tamten / tamta / tamto*, but in everyday speech Poles much more often just use *ten* and point.

The last row shows something typically Polish: a group that **includes men** is treated differently from other groups. This pattern comes back in the past tense (Unit 17). Just recognize it; you don't need to use it yet.

blocks.text: Grouped by gender so your eyes get used to the pattern instead of memorizing a random list.

blocks.title: Eye training: three seconds per word
items: Cover the header row, then read down the list saying *ten*, *ta*, or *to* before each word.
If in doubt, don't think too long — look at the last letter. Ending in *-a*: almost certainly *ta*; ending in *-o* or *-e*: almost certainly *to*; everything else: *ten*.
Repeat this once a day for a week. After that, noun gender stops being memorization and starts being a reflex.

blocks.text: A pattern that saves memorizing: 11–19 all end in **-naście**, which comes from "on top of ten" — like English *-teen*. Just know 1–10, then add the ending: *cztery → czternaście*, *sześć → szesnaście*.

blocks.title: Numbers and nouns — an early warning
items: A noun after a number **changes its form**, and the rule is unlike any language you know: *jeden bilet*, *dwa bilety*, but *pięć biletów*.
Don't deal with it now. All you need in this unit are the numbers themselves; the nouns are handled in Units 6 and 15.
To ask about quantity, use *ile?* — *Ile to kosztuje?* (how much does it cost?), *Ile masz lat?* (how old are you?).

exercises.prompt: Write the numbers out in words.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: ten — ta — to — ta — ten — to
